gloss: dried sweets; dry confections (traditional Japanese sweets with very low moisture content)

definitions.gloss: dried sweets; dry confections (a category of traditional Japanese sweets with low moisture content and long shelf life)
definitions.explanation: A category of traditional Japanese sweets ({和菓子|わがし}) characterized by very low moisture content (typically under 10%), giving them a hard, dry texture and a long shelf life. Common examples include {落雁|らくがん} (pressed sugar-and-rice-flour cakes), {金平糖|こんぺいとう} (small star-shaped sugar candies), {煎餅|せんべい} (in the sweet variety), and various sugar-coated and roasted sweets. They are especially associated with the formal tea ceremony, where they are served with {濃茶|こいちゃ} (thick tea) and high-grade matcha.

examples.japanese: {干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}を{食|た}べる。
{抹茶|まっちゃ}と{一緒|いっしょ}に{干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}が{出|だ}された。
examples.english: Dried sweets were served together with the matcha.

examples.japanese: この{店|みせ}の{干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}は{保存|ほぞん}が{利|き}くので、お{土産|みやげ}にぴったりだ。
examples.english: This shop's dried sweets keep well, so they're perfect as a souvenir.

examples.japanese: {茶会|ちゃかい}では、{濃茶|こいちゃ}の{前|まえ}に{季節|きせつ}の{花|はな}をかたどった{干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}が{丁寧|ていねい}に{並|なら}べられていた。
examples.english: At the tea ceremony, dried sweets shaped to resemble seasonal flowers were carefully arranged before the thick tea.

notes:
{干|ほ}し{菓子|がし} is the traditional Japanese category of sweets characterized by very low moisture content, in contrast to {生菓子|なまがし} ("fresh sweets") which are moist and perishable.

FORMATION:
- {干|ほ}し ("dried") + {菓子|がし} ("sweet, confection") → {干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}
- The {菓子|かし} component voices to {がし} as the second element of a compound (rendaku).

DEFINING FEATURES:
- Moisture content typically under about 10%
- Hard, dry, or brittle texture
- Long shelf life — often months at room temperature
- Frequently molded or shaped into seasonal motifs (flowers, leaves, animals)

COMMON EXAMPLES:
- {落雁|らくがん}: pressed cakes of fine sugar and rice flour
- {金平糖|こんぺいとう}: small, star-shaped sugar candies (originally Portuguese)
- {煎餅|せんべい}: sweet rice crackers (the sweet sugar-coated kind)
- {有平糖|あるへいとう}: pulled and twisted sugar candy
- {州浜|すはま}: roasted soybean flour sweets

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}を{出|だ}す: to serve dried sweets
- {干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}を{詰|つ}め{合|あ}わせる: to assemble an assortment of dried sweets
- {季節|きせつ}の{干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}: seasonal dried sweets
- {茶会|ちゃかい}の{干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}: dried sweets for a tea ceremony

SIMILAR / RELATED TERMS:
- {生菓子|なまがし}: "fresh sweets" — moist sweets with high water content (e.g., {大福|だいふく}, {練|ね}り{切|き}り); short shelf life
- {半生菓子|はんなまがし}: "semi-dry sweets" — intermediate moisture content (e.g., {最中|もなか})
- {和菓子|わがし}: Japanese-style sweets — the broader category that includes {干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}, {生菓子|なまがし}, and {半生菓子|はんなまがし}
- {落雁|らくがん}: a specific kind of {干|ほ}し{菓子|がし} made from sugar and rice flour

TEA-CEREMONY CONTEXT:
- In a formal tea ceremony, {干|ほ}し{菓子|がし} accompany {濃茶|こいちゃ} (thick tea) or are served at less formal points in the gathering.
- The sweets are often arranged on a flat tray ({干|ほ}し{菓子|がし}{盆|ぼん} or {菓子器|かしき}) and chosen to reflect the season.

USAGE NOTES:
- The reading {ほしがし} (with rendaku) is standard; {ほしかし} without voicing is non-standard.
- The same kanji {菓子|かし} appears in many compounds: {和菓子|わがし}, {洋菓子|ようがし}, {駄菓子|だがし}, etc.
